title: Diffusion, Osmosis & Active Transport
description: Diffusion and the factors that change its rate, water as a solvent, osmosis through partially permeable membranes with the required practicals, and an introduction to active transport for IGCSE Biology 0610.

notes.heading: Diffusion: The Core Definition
notes.body:
📌 Definition
**Diffusion** is the net movement of particles (molecules or ions) from a region of their **higher concentration** to a region of their **lower concentration**, down a **concentration gradient**, as a result of the **random movement** of the particles.

🔑 How it works
Particles never sit still — they are in constant random motion because of their own **kinetic energy**. Diffusion needs NO energy from the cell: the movement is powered entirely by the particles' own kinetic energy. Random motion sends particles in all directions, but MORE move away from where they are crowded than back towards it — so the NET movement is down the gradient, until concentrations even out.

🔑 What the examiner wants
The four load-bearing words: **net movement**, **higher to lower concentration**, **concentration gradient**, **random movement**. 'Particles move from high to low concentration' without 'net' or 'random' often loses the mark.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying diffusion 'requires energy'. It does not require METABOLIC energy (no respiration involved) — the energy comes from the kinetic energy of the molecules and ions themselves.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Net movement, high → low concentration, down the gradient.
• Driven by random motion and the particles' own kinetic energy — passive, no cell energy.

notes.heading: Why Diffusion Matters to Organisms
notes.body:
📌 Substances enter and leave cells across the cell membrane, and much of that traffic is by diffusion.

🔑 Gases
• **Oxygen** diffuses from the air in the lungs (high concentration) into the blood (low concentration), and from the blood into respiring cells.
• **Carbon dioxide** diffuses the opposite way — out of respiring cells, into the blood, and out of the lungs.
• In leaves, carbon dioxide diffuses IN through the stomata for photosynthesis, and oxygen (a product) diffuses OUT.

🔑 Dissolved substances (solutes)
• **Glucose** and other small food molecules diffuse from the small intestine into the blood.
• **Urea**, a waste product, diffuses from cells into the blood plasma for removal by the kidneys.

🔑 The pattern to quote
For every example, the answer frame is the same: 'X diffuses from [region of higher concentration] to [region of lower concentration], down its concentration gradient, across [the membrane/surface named].'

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing that oxygen diffuses OUT of the blood into the lungs. Always anchor the direction to where each gas is being made or used: respiring cells USE oxygen (so it diffuses in) and MAKE carbon dioxide (so it diffuses out).

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Diffusion moves O₂, CO₂, glucose and urea where organisms need them moved.
• Direction = from higher concentration to lower concentration, every time.

notes.heading: The Four Factors That Change the Rate of Diffusion
notes.body:
📌 The factors (0610 Core — you must be able to INVESTIGATE them)
• **Surface area** — a larger surface lets more particles cross at once → faster diffusion. Alveoli, root hairs and the small intestine lining all have huge surface areas for this reason.
• **Temperature** — warmer particles have more kinetic energy and move faster → faster diffusion.
• **Concentration gradient** — a STEEPER gradient (bigger difference between the two regions) → faster net movement.
• **Distance** — a shorter diffusion path → faster diffusion. This is why exchange surfaces are thin, and why large organisms cannot rely on diffusion alone and need transport systems.

🔑 Investigating them
• Gradient/temperature: time how long a coloured solute (e.g. a dye or potassium manganate(VII)) takes to spread through water or agar at different temperatures or starting concentrations.
• Surface area and distance: cut indicator-containing agar into cubes of different sizes, stand them in acid, and time how long each takes to change colour throughout — small cubes change first because the acid has less far to travel to the centre.
• Change ONE factor at a time; keep the others constant.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Claiming a steeper gradient changes the FINAL concentration — it only changes the SPEED. Diffusion still stops (net movement ends) when concentrations equalise.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Faster with: bigger surface area, higher temperature, steeper gradient, shorter distance.
• Investigate one variable at a time.

notes.heading: Water: The Solvent of Life
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A **solvent** is a liquid that dissolves other substances (the solutes) to form a solution. Water is the solvent in which the chemistry of living things happens — so many processes depend on substances being dissolved in it.

🔑 The three roles on the 0610 Core list
• **Digestion** — food molecules are broken down and carried in solution; enzymes work on dissolved substrates, and the small soluble products of digestion dissolve for absorption into the blood.
• **Excretion** — waste such as urea is removed dissolved in water, as urine.
• **Transport** — blood plasma (mostly water) carries dissolved glucose, amino acids, mineral ions, hormones and carbon dioxide around the body; in plants, water in the xylem carries dissolved mineral ions.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Treating 'water is a solvent' as a vague background fact. The syllabus expects you to attach it to named processes — digestion, excretion, transport — with an example of WHAT is dissolved in each.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Water = the solvent for digestion, excretion and transport.
• Name the solute in each example (digested food molecules, urea, mineral ions).

notes.heading: Osmosis: The Definition and What Moves
notes.body:
📌 Definition
**Osmosis** is the net movement of **water molecules** from a region of **higher water concentration** (a dilute solution) to a region of **lower water concentration** (a concentrated solution), through a **partially permeable membrane**.

🔑 How it works
• A **partially permeable membrane** lets small molecules (water) pass but holds back larger solute molecules — the cell membrane is one.
• Only the WATER makes the net journey; the solute stays put. Adding solute to water LOWERS the water concentration, so 'concentrated salt solution' = 'low water concentration'.
• Water can move INTO cells (dilute surroundings) or OUT of cells (concentrated surroundings) — always towards the lower water concentration.

🔑 What the examiner wants
State the direction in terms of WATER concentration, name the membrane as partially permeable, and use 'net movement'. (The water-potential terminology used to explain this more precisely is in the plant physiology topic — not needed at Core.)

⚠️ Common Mistake
Defining osmosis as 'movement from dilute to concentrated solution' without saying it is the WATER that moves. Salt does not diffuse out to meet the water halfway in these answers — the membrane holds it back.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Osmosis = water only, through a partially permeable membrane.
• Net movement is towards the region of lower water concentration (the more concentrated solution).

notes.heading: Osmosis Practicals and Plant Support
notes.body:
🔑 Required practical 1 — dialysis tubing (a model partially permeable membrane)
Fill dialysis tubing with a solution containing glucose and starch, seal it, and stand it in water. Test the water later: Benedict's test (heated) turns brick-red — glucose escaped; iodine stays brown — starch did NOT. The small glucose molecules passed through the membrane; the large starch molecules could not. This shows the membrane is PARTIALLY permeable.

🔑 Required practical 2 — plant tissue in different concentrations
Cut potato cylinders, measure the mass (or length) of each, and stand them in water and in salt/sugar solutions of different concentrations. After a set time, re-measure.
• Dilute solution (higher water concentration than the cells) → water ENTERS by osmosis → mass INCREASES, cylinders feel firm.
• Concentrated solution (lower water concentration) → water LEAVES → mass DECREASES, cylinders feel limp.
• No change in mass → the solution has the same water concentration as the cell contents — no net movement.

🔑 Plant support
Water entering plant cells pushes the cell contents against the cell wall; the wall resists, and the resulting pressure keeps cells firm. Millions of firm cells pressing on their walls is what holds non-woody stems and leaves upright — when water is short, cells lose this pressure and the plant wilts.

⚠️ Common Mistake
In the potato practical, describing mass gain as 'the potato absorbing salt'. The mass change is WATER moving by osmosis; the solute stays outside.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Dialysis tubing: small molecules through, large molecules held back.
• Potato cylinders: mass up = water in (dilute outside); mass down = water out (concentrated outside).
• Water pressure against cell walls supports the plant.

illustration.alt: Three panels showing a plant cell in distilled water, in a solution of matching concentration, and in concentrated salt solution, with arrows showing water entering, no net movement, and water leaving.
illustration.caption: Water moves by osmosis towards the lower water concentration: in when the surroundings are dilute, out when they are concentrated, and no net movement when concentrations match.

notes.heading: Active Transport: The Introduction
notes.body:
📌 Definition
**Active transport** is the movement of particles through a cell membrane from a region of **lower concentration** to a region of **higher concentration** — AGAINST the concentration gradient — using **energy from respiration**.

🔑 How it differs from diffusion and osmosis
• Diffusion and osmosis are PASSIVE: down the gradient, powered by the particles' own kinetic energy, no respiration needed.
• Active transport is ACTIVE: up the gradient, and it stops if respiration stops (for example, without oxygen).

💡 Worked Example
Root hair cells take up mineral ions from the soil even when the soil concentration is LOWER than inside the cell. Diffusion could never do this — it only runs downhill — so the cell uses active transport, powered by energy released in respiration (one reason root cells carry many mitochondria).

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing that active transport 'needs energy' without naming the source. The mark-scheme phrase is **energy from respiration**. (Why cells need active transport and the carrier proteins involved are Supplement detail — covered in the plant physiology topic, not at Core.)

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Active transport = against the gradient, using energy from respiration.
• Diffusion and osmosis = down the gradient, no metabolic energy.

flashcards.definition: The net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, down a concentration gradient, as a result of their random movement.
flashcards.example: Oxygen diffuses from the air in the alveoli into the blood, where its concentration is lower.

flashcards.definition: The difference in concentration between two regions. A steeper gradient gives faster diffusion; diffusion stops (net) when concentrations equalise.
flashcards.example: Respiring cells keep using oxygen, maintaining a steep gradient that draws more oxygen in from the blood.

flashcards.definition: The net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water concentration to a region of lower water concentration through a partially permeable membrane.
flashcards.example: Water enters root hair cells from the dilute soil water by osmosis.

flashcards.definition: A membrane that allows small molecules such as water to pass but blocks larger solute molecules. The cell membrane is one; dialysis tubing is a model of one.
flashcards.example: Glucose passes through dialysis tubing but starch cannot.

flashcards.definition: Tubing filled with glucose + starch solution is stood in water; glucose diffuses out (brick-red with heated Benedict's) but starch does not (iodine stays brown) — proving partial permeability.
flashcards.example: The tubing models how a cell membrane selects which molecules can cross.

flashcards.definition: A larger surface area increases the rate of diffusion because more particles can cross at the same time.
flashcards.example: Alveoli and root hair cells have large surface areas for fast exchange.

flashcards.definition: Higher temperature increases the kinetic energy of particles, so they move faster and diffuse faster.
flashcards.example: A dye spreads through warm water faster than through cold water.

flashcards.definition: The shorter the distance particles must travel, the faster diffusion completes — why exchange surfaces are thin and large organisms need transport systems.
flashcards.example: In an agar-cube experiment, the smallest cube changes colour throughout first.

flashcards.definition: Water dissolves substances so they can be digested, transported and excreted: digested food molecules in solution, urea in urine, mineral ions in xylem and blood plasma.
flashcards.example: Urea is removed from the body dissolved in water, as urine.

flashcards.definition: Water entering a plant cell pushes the contents against the cell wall; the resulting pressure keeps cells firm and supports non-woody parts of the plant.
flashcards.example: Watered plants stand upright; short of water the cells lose pressure and the plant wilts.

flashcards.definition: The movement of particles through a cell membrane from a lower to a higher concentration — against the gradient — using energy from respiration.
flashcards.example: Root hair cells absorb mineral ions from very dilute soil solution by active transport.

flashcards.definition: The energy of movement that all molecules and ions possess; it powers diffusion and osmosis, so these processes need no energy from respiration.
flashcards.example: A crystal of potassium manganate(VII) colours a whole beaker of still water without any stirring.

choices: The net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, down a concentration gradient, as a result of their random movement
The movement of water through a partially permeable membrane
The movement of particles from a low to a high concentration using energy from respiration
The spreading of particles caused by stirring or currents in the liquid
questions.explanation: The syllabus definition has four parts: net movement, higher to lower concentration, down the gradient, random movement. The water definition is osmosis; moving against the gradient with energy is active transport.

questions.stem: Where does the energy for diffusion come from?
choices: Respiration in the mitochondria of the cells
The kinetic energy of the moving molecules and ions themselves
Light energy absorbed by the membrane
Energy released when the concentration gradient forms
questions.explanation: Diffusion is passive: it is driven by the constant random motion of particles, i.e. their own kinetic energy. No respiration or other metabolic energy is involved.

questions.stem: Which change would increase the rate at which oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood?
choices: Making the alveolus walls thicker
Lowering the temperature of the body
Breathing air with a higher oxygen concentration, steepening the concentration gradient
Reducing the surface area of the alveoli
questions.explanation: A steeper concentration gradient increases the rate of net movement. Thicker walls increase the diffusion distance, and lower temperature or smaller surface area all slow diffusion down.

questions.stem: Small organisms such as an amoeba can rely on diffusion to supply oxygen to all their cells, but a human cannot. What is the best explanation?
choices: Humans have a lower respiration rate than amoebas
Diffusion only works in water, and humans live on land
Amoebas carry out active transport instead of diffusion
In a large organism the diffusion distance from the surface to the innermost cells is too great for diffusion alone to supply them fast enough
questions.explanation: Diffusion rate falls sharply with distance. A single-celled organism is only micrometres across, so diffusion suffices; a human's innermost cells are centimetres from any surface, so a circulatory system is needed to bring oxygen close to every cell.

choices: The net movement of solute molecules across a cell membrane
The net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water concentration to a region of lower water concentration through a partially permeable membrane
The movement of water from a concentrated solution to a dilute solution
The uptake of water by a cell using energy from respiration
questions.explanation: Osmosis is about WATER only, moving towards the lower water concentration (the more concentrated solution) through a partially permeable membrane. It is passive — respiration energy belongs to active transport.

choices: A membrane that lets all substances pass through slowly
A membrane that lets nothing pass through
A membrane that allows small molecules such as water to pass but blocks larger solute molecules
A membrane found only in plant cells
questions.explanation: Partial permeability is selective: water crosses, larger solute molecules are held back. It is the property that makes osmosis possible, and the cell membrane of every cell has it.

questions.stem: Dialysis tubing containing a solution of glucose and starch is sealed and stood in pure water. After 20 minutes the water gives a brick-red result with heated Benedict's solution but stays brown with iodine. What does this show?
choices: Starch diffused out but glucose did not
Both glucose and starch diffused out of the tubing
Nothing crossed the tubing — the tests are negative
The small glucose molecules passed through the partially permeable membrane, but the larger starch molecules could not
questions.explanation: Brick-red Benedict's detects glucose in the water outside; brown iodine shows no starch left the tubing. Only the small molecules crossed — exactly what 'partially permeable' means.

questions.stem: A potato cylinder gains mass in distilled water but loses mass in a concentrated salt solution. Why?
choices: In distilled water the higher water concentration outside drives water into the cells by osmosis; in salt solution the lower water concentration outside draws water out
Salt diffuses into the potato, making it lighter
The potato cells respire faster in salt solution, using up mass
Distilled water dissolves the potato's starch, increasing its mass
questions.explanation: Mass changes are water moving by osmosis towards the region of lower water concentration: in from dilute surroundings, out to concentrated surroundings. The salt itself stays outside the cells.

questions.stem: How does water support the non-woody parts of a plant?
choices: Water in the xylem is stiff and holds the plant up like a skeleton
Water makes the cell walls grow thicker and stronger
Water entering the cells pushes the contents against the cell walls, and the pressure keeps the cells firm
Water sticks the cells of the stem together
questions.explanation: Water entering by osmosis presses the cell contents against the wall, which resists; this pressure keeps every cell firm, and millions of firm cells hold the stem and leaves upright. Water shortage removes the pressure — the plant wilts.

questions.stem: Urea is removed from the body dissolved in water, as urine. Which role of water does this illustrate?
choices: Digestion
Transport
Photosynthesis
Excretion
questions.explanation: Urea is a waste product of metabolism, and carrying it out of the body in solution is excretion — one of the three solvent roles on the syllabus (digestion, excretion, transport). Photosynthesis is how plants gain materials, not a solvent role of water.

questions.stem: Agar cubes containing universal indicator are cut to 1 cm, 2 cm and 3 cm side lengths and dropped into dilute acid at the same time. Which cube changes colour completely first, and why?
choices: The 1 cm cube — the acid has the shortest distance to diffuse to reach the centre
The 3 cm cube — it has the largest surface area for the acid to enter
All at the same time — the acid diffuses at the same speed whatever the cube size
The 2 cm cube — it has the best balance of surface area and volume
questions.explanation: Acid diffuses at the same rate into all three, but the distance to the centre is least in the smallest cube, so it is neutralised throughout first. This experiment models why diffusion distance matters — and why big organisms need transport systems.

questions.stem: How does active transport differ from diffusion?
choices: Active transport moves particles down the concentration gradient; diffusion moves them against it
Active transport moves particles from a lower to a higher concentration, against the gradient, using energy from respiration; diffusion moves them down the gradient with no metabolic energy
Active transport moves only water; diffusion moves only solutes
There is no difference — both are passive processes
questions.explanation: Active transport runs uphill against the gradient and needs energy from respiration; diffusion runs downhill on the particles' own kinetic energy. Root hair cells absorbing mineral ions from very dilute soil water is the standard example of active transport.

questions.stem: Red blood cells are placed in a concentrated salt solution. What happens, and why?
choices: They swell and may burst, because water enters by osmosis
Nothing — blood cells are surrounded by a cell wall
Salt enters the cells by diffusion until the concentrations match
They shrink, because the salt solution has a lower water concentration than the cells, so water leaves by osmosis
questions.explanation: The concentrated solution outside has a lower water concentration than the cytoplasm, so the net movement of water is OUT of the cells through the partially permeable membrane, and they shrink. Animal cells have no cell wall — in distilled water they would swell and burst.

questions.stem: Which of these does NOT affect the rate of diffusion?
choices: The colour of the solution
The temperature
The concentration gradient
The surface area across which diffusion occurs
questions.explanation: The four factors are surface area, temperature, concentration gradient and distance. Colour makes a solute easier to track in an experiment but has no effect on how fast the particles move.

questions.stem: A student masses potato cylinders, stands each one in a solution of a different concentration, and re-masses them after 30 minutes. The cylinder in solution X has not changed mass. What is the best conclusion?
choices: Solution X is pure water
Osmosis did not occur in solution X because the membrane failed
Solution X has the same water concentration as the potato cell contents, so there was no net movement of water
The cylinder in solution X was dead, so no osmosis was possible
questions.explanation: Osmosis still occurs — water crosses in both directions — but with equal water concentrations the movements balance, so NET movement is zero and mass is unchanged. The concentration at which mass change is zero estimates the water concentration inside the cells.
